kernel: A ghost story that is funny and frightening in equal measure. You inherit a decrepit canal boat with a resident ghost who insists he is still the captain and will not let the boat leave its mooring. Your only living companion is your brother-in-law, who came to help you sell it and who wants his money back more than he wants you safe. I want the ghost to be a real character, scary when he needs to be, and I want the boat to actually go somewhere.

shape.note: through_lines is how many distinct story lines (each with its own ending) the shape preference suggests; the review decides whether each next one is worth building.

protagonist.who: You are the new owner of a narrow, leaking narrowboat, the only living person aboard while a dead captain still keeps the log.
protagonist.history: You inherited the boat from your late sister, who kept it as a summer house and left you the keys, the unpaid canal dues, and a brother-in-law who paid to clear the title and now wants that money back.
protagonist.wants: to get the boat under way and to a place where it can be sold before your brother-in-law's patience runs out.
protagonist.need: to find out whether owning a boat means you can move it, or whether you must answer to everyone who ever kept it.
protagonist.can_do: steer when the wheel will turn, re-tie the mooring line if it lets you, read the logbook, talk to the ghost and your brother-in-law, carry the sale papers and coins, set the galley table, and make the boat physically ready to move.
protagonist.cannot_do: make the ghost obey, cut the mooring line while it is bound, sell the boat without a buyer reaching the stern, or move the boat without the wheel, ropes, and line cooperating.

ties.what: your sister's husband, the man who paid to clear the title and now counts every coin as if your safety were a line item.
the dead man in the rotting uniform who still checks the logs and complains about the bilge water as if you were both still on duty.

protagonist.open: whether you learn to command the boat as a living owner or let the dead captain's protocol decide your terms.
protagonist.name: Ingrid Kowalczyk

arena.description: A decrepit narrowboat moored stern-to-towpath on a quiet canal, with a narrow stern deck at the mooring ring, a low-ceilinged galley, and a bow where the mooring line is tied to a bollard.

pressure.description: Your brother-in-law will not wait past the evening to see the boat sold, and the canal's low water is already pulling at the hull as if the boat were meant to move tonight.
pressure.clock_or_stock: none tracked; the urgency is told through the brother-in-law's impatience, the falling light, and the water's pull, because 3-0c names no failure trigger

opposition.wants: to remain the boat's captain and to have it move only under his orders, with the logbook kept true and the bilge water answered to.
opposition.means: he can seize the steering wheel, tighten the ropes, make the mooring line refuse the knife, set the galley table, stand behind you where the light will not hold, and speak with his mouth slightly out of sync with his voice.

events.what: A distant walker stops at the stern mooring ring and asks if the boat is for sale; your brother-in-law begins a bargain while the ghost stands directly behind you, blocking the view of the boat's interior.
The galley table sets itself for a meal the ghost insists on eating, and your brother-in-law's sandwich keeps sliding off the plate under the low ceiling.

The mooring line at the bow snaps not with a bang but with a wet, organic sound, as if it were a tendon, and the boat slips into the current; just below the hull, the ghost's face looks up, not angry but disappointed.

mediation.question: Who has the right to make this boat move: the dead captain who keeps the log, or the living owner who holds the key?

to_reach_pole_a.what_you_must_do: let him remain captain: acknowledge his authority in the logbook, set the galley table for his meal, use the brass whistle to give the order to move, and let him choose the first leg of the journey.
to_reach_pole_a.cost: you surrender some of your ownership, your brother-in-law watches you bargain with a corpse and doubts the sale, and the boat moves on the dead man's schedule rather than yours.

to_reach_pole_b.what_you_must_do: work around or defy the ghost: get the sale papers and your brother-in-law's coins into your hands, find a buyer or passerby who will pay for the boat as property, and physically free the mooring line, the wheel, or the ropes so the boat moves without his order.
to_reach_pole_b.cost: the boat resists with tightening ropes, a seizing wheel, and a mooring line that will not cut, and your brother-in-law's safety and patience are tested as the cold and the dark close in.

framework.name: Kishotenketsu
framework.shape: a situation is introduced and deepened without conflict, an unexpected element recasts it, and the two are reconciled

modifier.name: Episodic middle
modifier.effect: Each middle beat is a self-contained instance of the story's recurring decision with its own small ending; what carries across them is what the protagonist is becoming.

framework.reading: The story opens with the boat stuck and the living wanting to sell it, then escalates through escalating, self-contained hauntings and bargaining attempts that deepen the absurdity rather than the danger. It should land on the boat actually moving, not because the ghost is defeated, but because the situation resolves into a comic, uneasy success where the dead captain's authority is acknowledged in a way that lets the living move forward.
framework.why: Its four-beat structure matches the brief's 'sustained' trajectory (3b.primary_trajectory) and 'none' failure presence (3-0c.failure_presence), where the conflict is a negotiation rather than a hard defeat. The 'Turn' (ten) aligns with the engine's 'confront' turn where the line snaps, and the 'Reconciliation' (ketsu) matches the 'comic, uneasy success' (3c.moral_valence) where the boat moves and the brother-in-law's money is addressed, rather than a climactic battle.

beats.name: Introduction (ki)
beats.job: the people and the place at rest: what an ordinary day here is

beats.name: Development (sho)
beats.job: the same situation, deepened: more of what was introduced, with no new conflict required

beats.name: Turn (ten)
beats.job: an unexpected element or viewpoint that recasts what came before

beats.name: Reconciliation (ketsu)
beats.job: the turn and the earlier material are brought together into a new whole

T1.title: The First Leg
T1.motivation: You start out needing to sell the boat before Ivo Gutierrez’s patience runs out, and by the end you are trying to learn whether a living owner can make a dead man’s vessel move without becoming his clerk.
T1.strategy: Keep the sale papers, the coins, and the buyer in front of you, and meet the ghost captain’s protocol only far enough to make the boat obey.
T1.turning_point: The distant walker, Kwame Nakashima, agrees to buy only if he can see the boat move; from then on, the sale and the first leg become the same action.

ending.title: A Sold Boat Under a Dead Captain’s Keel
ending.summary: The boat leaves the mooring and begins its first leg with the sale papers signed at the stern, the coins in Ivo Gutierrez’s wet hand, and Pieter Oyelaran’s face looking up from the water with disappointment rather than anger. It costs you the clean authority of ownership: the boat moves, but it moves on terms the dead man helped write.
ending.changed: the boat is sold, under way, and no longer yours to command alone

T2.title: The Bilge Answer
T2.motivation: You start out needing to sell the boat before Ivo Gutierrez's patience runs out, but after answering Pieter Oyelaran's complaint about the unsounded bilge and feeling the wheel seize in your hand while Ivo Gutierrez's coin purse slips into the water, you come to want the dead captain's terms to be the only terms that work. By the end you want the boat moving and sold, even if that means the sale is made under Pieter Oyelaran's captaincy and Ivo Gutierrez is left with no share.
T2.strategy: Keep the logbook, the brass whistle, and the meal in front of you; satisfy Pieter Oyelaran's standing orders; let Kwame Nakashima agree to buy the boat on faith while the ghost blocks the view; and move Ivo Gutierrez out of the way of the protocol until he leaves the boat of his own accord.
T2.turning_point: The coin purse in the bilge. Once Ivo Gutierrez's money is gone and the wheel answers only while Pieter Oyelaran is speaking, the sale papers stop being enough; the logbook becomes the only instrument that can make the boat move.
T2.differs_from: T1 answers the question in mixed terms, keeps Ivo Gutierrez standing at the stern with wet sale papers, and leaves Pieter Oyelaran disappointed in the water; this line answers with pole_a, keeps the dead captain standing as the boat's effective captain, and loses Ivo Gutierrez, who walks off the towpath before the boat moves.

ending.title: The Bilge Answer
ending.summary: At first light the boat moves under Pieter Oyelaran's log entry and whistle call. Kwame Nakashima pays at the stern for a boat he bought on faith, and Ivo Gutierrez is left on the towpath with his coin purse gone and no share of the sale. The boat goes under the dead captain's first leg, with the logbook still open and the ghost keeping the wheel.
ending.changed: the boat is sold as a captain's vessel with the logbook still open and the dead captain's terms governing the first leg

divergence.trigger: you answered Pieter Oyelaran's complaint about the unsounded bilge and let the wheel seize in your hand while Ivo Gutierrez's coin purse slipped into the bilge
divergence.instead_of: you read the standing orders from the logbook and learned that the wheel would answer only after a log entry, a whistle call, and a meal were set
divergence.opportunity: Ivo Gutierrez's coin purse must be on the stern deck near the bilge, with the brass whistle in it, so that it can slip into the water when the wheel seizes.
divergence.shift: The wheel answers only while you are speaking to the dead captain, and the living owner's money is already under the hull. Pieter Oyelaran's complaint has become a working instruction, and Ivo Gutierrez's practical leverage is gone.

T2.why: The seed holds as given: N02's unused way 2 makes the living owner's money go into the bilge and leaves the logbook as the only working order. That change lets the line move toward pole_a without retelling T1: the sale is still made at the stern, but the buyer is won by faith rather than by the logbook's terms, Ivo's breaking point is crossed in the galley, and the boat finally moves under the dead captain's whistle call with Ivo already lost on the towpath.

T3.title: The Owner's Key
T3.motivation: You come to want the sale papers to matter more than the ghost's protocol, because Ivo Gutierrez's ruined sandwich and cold face make clear that the boat is becoming a set of standing orders before it becomes a sale; by the end you want the boat moved and sold under your own key as an ordinary owner, even if that leaves Pieter Oyelaran facing the stern with his log closed.
T3.strategy: Call the ghost's meal off with the brass whistle, keep Ivo Gutierrez at the sale papers, write your own log entry, and free the bow line so the boat moves under Ingrid Kowalczyk's key before Pieter Oyelaran can face the wheel again.
T3.turning_point: The brass whistle in your hand: when you cancel the meal, the galley stops being Pieter Oyelaran's protocol and becomes your sale, and the logbook stops being only his record.
T3.differs_from: T1: T1 moves the boat on mixed terms with the dead captain's help, while this line answers pole_b by selling the boat as an ordinary narrowboat and letting Ingrid Kowalczyk choose the first leg. T2: T2 lets the dead captain's terms become the only terms and loses Ivo Gutierrez, while this line keeps Ivo Gutierrez at the sale papers and rejects Pieter Oyelaran's captaincy in favor of the living owner's key.

ending.title: The Owner's Key
ending.summary: The boat moves under Ingrid Kowalczyk's key and her own log entry, and Kwame Nakashima pays for an ordinary narrowboat rather than a captain's vessel. Ivo Gutierrez gets his money back and stands with the sale papers dry, while Pieter Oyelaran is left facing the stern with the logbook closed. The price is the dead captain's claim: the ropes cut your hands, the cold stays in the hull, and the boat no longer moves on his schedule.
ending.changed: the boat is sold as an ordinary narrowboat and Ingrid Kowalczyk chooses the first leg

divergence.trigger: you used the brass whistle to call Pieter Oyelaran's meal off and made the set table stop moving
divergence.instead_of: you set the table for Pieter Oyelaran's meal and let the plates stop moving

T3.why: The seed holds as given: calling the meal off with the brass whistle is turn 3's unused way 3 at N04, and it changes the boat's movement from Pieter Oyelaran's protocol into Ingrid Kowalczyk's sale. The seed's ending world holds because the line can keep Ivo Gutierrez at the sale papers, sell to Kwame Nakashima as an ordinary narrowboat, and leave Pieter Oyelaran without the logbook's authority.

promises.reading: This is a gothic comedy set on the water: a haunted vessel that refuses to move because its dead captain still believes he is in command. The writer wants the specific texture of a canal boat—the creaking wood, the narrow galley, the mist on the water—to ground the supernatural, and wants the fear to be real enough to make the humor land. They are hoping to feel the relief of a shared secret and the thrill of outwitting a stubborn authority figure who is also a monster.
promises.player_fantasy: To be the living owner of a place that refuses to obey you, armed only with logic, leverage, and a skeptical relative, while the walls close in and the dead man's grip tightens.

promises.tone_engine: Funny: the ghost is a stickler for protocol and the brother-in-law is a pragmatist; the comedy arises from the absurdity of negotiating with a corpse over property rights. Eerie: the cold is constant, the shadows move when they shouldn't, and the ghost's voice is always slightly out of sync with his mouth.
obligatory_cast: a canal towpath that is empty except for the occasional, distant walker who sees the boat but not the ghost
a specific, mundane object that serves as the ghost's 'anchor' to the boat, such as a brass whistle or a logbook that only he can read
must_not: no other ghosts or supernatural entities: the haunting is singular and personal to the captain
no modern technology that solves the problem instantly (e.g., a phone app to sell the boat): the solution must be physical and negotiated
no death of the living characters: the fear is sustained, not fatal, per the 'comic, uneasy success' trajectory
